title: Imports: Primes, Lattices, Tactics
content: Imports Mathlib modules for prime numbers, conditionally complete lattices (for sSup and BddAbove), and tactics. These provide the infrastructure for defining the Jacobsthal function via suprema over sets of natural numbers.
mathContext: The formalization uses `sSup` from `Order.ConditionallyCompleteLattice.Basic` to define $Y(x)$ and $g(n)$ as suprema. This requires showing the relevant sets are nonempty and bounded above.

title: Primorial P(x)
content: Defines **primorial(x)** = ∏_{p ≤ x, p prime} p, the product of all primes up to x. This is the modulus whose Jacobsthal function equals Y(x).
mathContext: The primorial $P(x) = \prod_{p \le x} p$ grows as $e^{(1+o(1))x}$ by the prime number theorem. It is the most 'efficient' number with many small prime factors, making $g(P(x))$ the extremal case of the Jacobsthal function.

title: Covering System
content: Defines **IsCovered(x, a, n)**: an integer n is covered if n ≡ aₚ (mod p) for some prime p ≤ x. The function a assigns a residue class to each prime, forming a covering system.
mathContext: A covering system assigns residue classes $\{a_p \pmod{p} \mid p \le x, p \text{ prime}\}$. An integer $n$ is covered if $n \in \bigcup_p (a_p + p\mathbb{Z})$. The question is: how long an initial interval $[1, y]$ can be covered?

title: Jacobsthal Set
content: Defines **jacobsthalSet(x)** as the set of all y such that some covering system for primes ≤ x covers every integer in [1, y]. The supremum of this set is Y(x).
mathContext: The set $\{y \mid \exists a, \forall n \in [1,y], n \text{ is covered by } a\}$ captures all achievable covering lengths. Its supremum $Y(x) = \sup(\text{jacobsthalSet}(x))$ is the extremal quantity.

title: Y(x) — Maximum Covering Length
content: Defines **jacobsthalY(x)** = sSup(jacobsthalSet(x)), the maximum y such that some covering system for primes ≤ x covers all integers in [1, y]. This is the central object of Problem #687.
mathContext: $Y(x) = \sup\{y \mid \exists \text{covering } a, [1,y] \subseteq \bigcup_p (a_p + p\mathbb{Z})\}$. The well-definedness requires `jacobsthalSet` to be nonempty and bounded above, both of which are established.

title: Jacobsthal Function g(n)
content: Defines **jacobsthal(n)** = sSup{d | ∃ m, ∀ k ∈ (m, m+d), ∃ prime p | n with p | k}. This is the largest gap between consecutive integers coprime to n, equivalently 1 plus the longest run of non-coprime integers.
mathContext: The Jacobsthal function $g(n) = \max\{d \mid \exists m, \text{gcd}(k, n) > 1 \text{ for all } m < k < m + d\}$ measures the largest gap in the integers coprime to $n$. For $n = P(x)$, this equals $Y(x)$.

title: Jacobsthal Set Nonempty
content: The jacobsthalSet is always nonempty: y = 0 is vacuously in the set since there are no integers in [1, 0]. This is needed to justify the use of sSup.
mathContext: The proof constructs $y = 0$ and any covering function $a$ (choosing $a_p = 0$ for all $p$). The covering condition $\forall n \in [1, 0]$ is vacuously true since $[1, 0] = \emptyset$.

title: Jacobsthal Set Bounded Above
content: The jacobsthalSet(x) is bounded above. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the covering pattern repeats with period primorial(x), so any uncovered integer implies infinitely many uncovered integers.
mathContext: By CRT, $\text{IsCovered}(x, a, n) \iff \text{IsCovered}(x, a, n + P(x))$. So if $[1, y]$ is covered, the pattern repeats but $y \le P(x)$ since eventually an uncovered residue class modulo $P(x)$ appears. Thus $Y(x) \le P(x)$.

title: Jacobsthal Set Monotonicity
content: If x₁ ≤ x₂ then jacobsthalSet(x₁) ⊆ jacobsthalSet(x₂). The proof extends any covering for primes ≤ x₁ to primes ≤ x₂ by assigning residue class 0 to each new prime.
mathContext: Given a covering $a$ for primes $\le x_1$, define $a'_p = a_p$ for $p \le x_1$ and $a'_p = 0$ for $x_1 < p \le x_2$. Any $n$ covered by $a$ is also covered by $a'$ (using the same prime $p \le x_1$). The new primes only help.

title: Y(x) Monotonicity
content: **Y(x) is monotone**: x₁ ≤ x₂ implies Y(x₁) ≤ Y(x₂). More primes allow longer covering intervals. Proved via csSup_le_csSup from the set monotonicity.
mathContext: From $\text{jacobsthalSet}(x_1) \subseteq \text{jacobsthalSet}(x_2)$ and both sets being nonempty and bounded above, `csSup_le_csSup` gives $\text{sSup}(\text{jacobsthalSet}(x_1)) \le \text{sSup}(\text{jacobsthalSet}(x_2))$.

title: Y(x) = g(primorial(x))
content: **Fundamental equivalence**: Y(x) equals the Jacobsthal function of the primorial. This connects covering systems (combinatorial) to gaps in coprime sequences (analytic).
mathContext: The integers not coprime to $P(x)$ are exactly those divisible by some prime $p \le x$. A covering system assigns residue classes to these primes. The maximum covered interval $Y(x)$ equals the maximum gap $g(P(x))$ between consecutive integers coprime to $P(x)$.

title: Erdős Problem #687 ($1,000 Prize)
content: **Main Conjecture**: For all ε > 0, eventually Y(x) ≤ x^{1+ε}. This asks whether Y(x) = o(x²), formalized using Lean's `Filter.Eventually` and `Filter.atTop`.
mathContext: The conjecture $Y(x) = o(x^2)$ is equivalent to: $\forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists X, \forall x \ge X, Y(x) \le x^{1+\varepsilon}$. The stronger form $Y(x) \le x^{1+o(1)}$ is formalized here. Even proving $Y(x) \le x^{2-\delta}$ for any fixed $\delta > 0$ would be a major advance.

title: Iwaniec Upper Bound (1978)
content: **Iwaniec's Theorem**: There exists C > 0 such that Y(x) ≤ C · x² for all x ≥ 2. This 1978 result remains the best known upper bound, unimproved for nearly 50 years.
mathContext: Iwaniec proved $g(n) \ll (\log n)^2$ for any $n$, which for $n = P(x)$ with $\log P(x) \sim x$ gives $Y(x) = g(P(x)) \ll x^2$. The proof uses the Selberg sieve: the number of integers in $[1, y]$ coprime to $P(x)$ is $\sim y/\log x$ by Mertens' theorem, so gaps of length $\gg x^2$ would leave too many uncovered integers.

title: FGKMT Lower Bound (2018)
content: **Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao**: Y(x) ≥ c · x · (log x)(log log log x)/(log log x). This improved Rankin's 1938 classical bound using breakthrough techniques from the proof of bounded gaps between primes.
mathContext: The FGKMT bound $Y(x) \gg x \cdot \frac{\log x \cdot \log \log \log x}{\log \log x}$ improves Rankin's $x \cdot \frac{\log x \cdot \log \log x \cdot \log \log \log \log x}{(\log \log \log x)^2}$ by a factor of $(\log \log \log x)^3 / (\log \log x \cdot \log \log \log \log x)$. Their method uses Maynard–Tao sieve weights and the Erdős–Rankin construction.

title: Maier–Pomerance Conjecture
content: **Conjectured**: Y(x) ≤ C · x · (log x)^{2+ε} for any ε > 0 and large x. If true, this would nearly close the gap with the FGKMT lower bound, leaving only a (log x)^{1+o(1)} factor.
mathContext: The Maier–Pomerance conjecture $Y(x) \ll x \cdot (\log x)^{2+o(1)}$ would imply $Y(x) = o(x^{1+\delta})$ for any $\delta > 0$, resolving Erdős's \$1,000 problem. It is based on probabilistic heuristics for the Jacobsthal function.

title: Trivial Lower Bound: Y(x) ≥ x + 1
content: For x ≥ 2, Y(x) ≥ x + 1. Every integer in [1, x] has a prime factor ≤ x, so taking aₚ = 0 for all primes p ≤ x covers at least [1, x].
mathContext: For any $n \in [1, x]$, the smallest prime factor of $n$ is $\le \sqrt{n} \le x$ (for $n \ge 2$), and $1$ is covered vacuously. Taking $a_p = 0$ gives $n \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ iff $p \mid n$, covering all of $[1, x]$.
